  trauma_type: Man-made disaster

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Event Recall: Talking about the event, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Friends: avoid seeing friends, Sit With Back to Wall: always sit with back against a wall to see the room, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled
  Memory: Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Vignette:
Tevita had always taken pride in his ability to stay calm under pressure. As a publisher, he was accustomed to meeting deadlines and juggling multiple projects at once. But everything changed on the day of the nightclub fire. Tevita had been attending a launch party for one of his company's new authors when the flames broke out, trapping him and dozens of others inside. The memories of that night are still etched vividly in his mind – the sound of shattering glass, the feeling of heat on his skin, the desperate scramble to find an exit. Tevita remembers the smell of alcohol-soaked carpets, which now makes his stomach turn whenever he catches a whiff of it. He recalls the sight of people screaming and crying, their faces illuminated only by the flickering lights of the club's emergency exits. In the months that followed, Tevita began to notice changes in himself. He would wake up from nightmares, drenched in sweat, with images of the fire still seared into his mind. He started avoiding social gatherings, including meetings with friends and colleagues, fearing that talking about the event would bring it all flooding back. His wife, Moana, grew concerned as Tevita became increasingly withdrawn, rarely leaving their home except to go to work. Even at the office, Tevita felt on edge. He would sit with his back against the wall, constantly scanning the room for potential threats – a habit he had developed in case another disaster struck. His colleagues began to notice his jumpiness, how he would startle at the slightest sound, whether it was the copier jamming or someone dropping a pen. Tevita's hypervigilance extended to his home life as well. He would find himself checking and rechecking the locks, the stove, the electrical outlets – anything that could potentially cause harm. Moana tried to reassure him, but Tevita couldn't shake the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. As time passed, Tevita's memories of the fire showed no signs of fading. Instead, they seemed to be growing more vivid, more intrusive. He would find himself reliving the experience at random moments – while driving, during meetings, even in his sleep. The images were so clear that he could almost smell the smoke and feel the heat on his skin. One night, Tevita woke up from a particularly intense nightmare, his heart racing and his sheets soaked with sweat. Moana was beside him, trying to calm him down, but Tevita knew he needed help. He couldn't keep living like this – always on edge, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. With Moana's encouragement, Tevita made an appointment with a therapist, hoping to find some way to quiet the memories and regain control over his life. As he sat in the therapist's office, Tevita felt a mix of emotions: fear, anxiety, but also a glimmer of hope. He was afraid of confronting the trauma head-on, but he knew he couldn't keep avoiding it forever. What he hoped for most was to learn how to live with his memories without being controlled by them – to find some way to put the fire behind him and move forward, once and for all.
